title: The Holiday Questions Korean Families Are Retiring

slides.headline: Korean relatives are asking **fewer questions** this Chuseok.
slides.note: The holiday used to come with an interrogation: exams, job, marriage, baby. That script is losing its grip.

slides.headline: It has a name: **janseori (잔소리)**
slides.body: Nagging from an elder. At Chuseok (추석) it arrives as questions about school, work, marriage and children.

slides.headline: The whole family lands in **one room**
slides.body: Relatives meet once or twice a year. Everything they missed gets asked in a single afternoon, oldest first.

slides.headline: The questions follow a **life schedule**
slides.body: Grades, then university, then a job, then a wedding, then a baby. Each visit checks the next box.

slides.headline: the joke price for **"when’s the wedding?"**
slides.body: A janseori price list charges relatives per question. It spread online as a printable, and families put it on the table.

slides.headline: They mean care. It lands as an **audit**
slides.body: Older relatives ask because they are interested. Asked in front of everyone, it still works like a public progress report.

slides.headline: The jobs came later. The weddings, **later still**
slides.body: A schedule built for a different economy keeps asking about milestones many people have pushed back or dropped.

slides.headline: Elsewhere you get asked **how you are**
slides.body: Here the question was about stage: what you have reached by now. That is the part families are quietly cutting.

slides.headline: Chuseok is becoming a **visit, not a review**
slides.body: Shorter gatherings, trips instead of the family house, and relatives who ask what you have been watching lately.

slides.headline: Korea, explained **by a Korean.**
slides.body: Follow for the context behind the things Korea does.

caption:
Korean holiday nagging has a name — janseori — and it is the round of questions relatives ask when the family gathers for Chuseok: your grades, your job, your wedding, your baby.

It was never meant as an attack. It is care running on a life schedule that was set decades ago, asked out loud in front of everyone. What is changing is how much of it survives the afternoon: shorter visits, families travelling instead, and a joke price list that lets everyone laugh the question off.

What does your family always ask when everyone is in the same room?
reply:
One thing that did not fit on the cards: the price list started as a joke image passed around online, and some families now print it and leave it on the table before the relatives arrive. It works because everyone gets to laugh at the same question instead of answering it.

What is the one question your family always asks when everyone is together?
